1#א: Glass. The reason is stated in the Taz that glass is also called metal, for it can be repaired by melting; and the reason for immersion is so that they emerge from the impurity of the non-Jew to the sanctity of Israel. Ohr U'Me'ir wrote that vessels coated with glass have the same law as vessels coated with lead.
1#ב: Blessing. Or he immerses them together with some other vessel with a blessing, as below seif 9 (Ohr U'Me'ir: for the coating on the inside is only for ornament; nevertheless, if coated inside and outside, everyone immerses it with a blessing — Peri Chadash). Mordechai wrote that even if it is coated only on the outside with lead, one immerses it without a blessing; Bach wrote that one should wonder at the custom of the world who use pots coated with lead on the inside without any immersion at all.
2#_: Detached water. The Taz disagrees and holds that even with detached water it is effective, provided only that he not grip the vessel forcefully but only with moderate contact — see there at length. Shach wrote that it requires study, for here the Mechaber plainly rules that if the vessel is loose in his hand at the time of immersion it is effective; yet Rambam in chapter 2 of Hilchot Mikvaot wrote that one who holds a person and vessels and immerses them — they remain in their impurity, and even if he loosened his hands it is a decree lest he not loosen; and Bach ruled in siman 198 seif 20 regarding immersion of a person that even if loose his immersion did not take effect; and in Mikvaot end of chapter 8 we plainly teach "a person and vessels together" — see there; requires study.
3#_: Vessels. Shach wrote that some poskim bless on immersion of metal vessels; Bach wrote that this is the essential practice and that he saw them act thus according to the elders; Taz wrote that one need not mention metal, and greater still he found at the end of Ohr U'Me'ir in a responsum: Mahari'z Ronkel answered that one should not mention "vessel" but only immerse plainly (b'dieved, if he blessed on many vessels "on immersion of a vessel," or on one vessel "on immersion of vessels," he has fulfilled — Peri Chadash).
4#_: Tripod. Meaning what they call in foreign tongue "dreifus" and "fiddleash" — meaning a trivet in foreign tongue, upon which they actually roast the food.
5#א: That they skin with it. Shach wrote the reason that they are not eating vessels, for the animal still requires cooking or roasting.
5#ב: Matzah irons. In this too one immerses without a blessing — Taz; but Shach wrote that those irons are even more inferior, since it is impossible to use them for another food, therefore they do not require immersion at all; accordingly it appears that vegetable scissors with which one trims them also do not require immersion, unlike Bach; and certainly the awl with which one pierces barrel hoops does not require immersion, and so is the practice; Ohr U'Me'ir wrote that likewise the iron with which one fixes "kreplekh" on Purim, or with which one scrapes dough in the kneading trough, does not require immersion — only if one removes burnt matter from bread when taking it from the oven does it require immersion.
6#_: Hoops. Meaning in foreign tongue "reifen"; Shach wrote requires study, for Beit Yosef ruled that one should immerse it without a blessing, for we are uncertain whether we follow the one who stabilizes it or not; therefore one immerses it without a blessing or with other vessels.
7#א: Immersion. It implies that a blessing is required; and even though Beit Yosef ruled regarding a silver cup whose stabilizer is wood that one immerses without a blessing, one may say that there, if not for the wood the cup would not be fit at all and the wood is what stabilizes it; but here the case is where the cup is fit as is and is only attached to a wooden vessel — end of Shach's words; and Taz explained another matter — see there.
7#ב: Iron. Ohr U'Me'ir wrote that the lower part that receives the grindings does not require immersion, for it is a wooden vessel; and a wooden funnel that has an iron tube does not require immersion even though one uses it via the iron, since it does not stabilize relative to the funnel; and likewise all similar cases — end of his words.
8#_: Cards. The same applies if he bought it for commerce; Shach ruled that one immerses it without a blessing, and likewise Taz; he further wrote that likewise one who borrows a vessel from a Jewish shopkeeper for a meal immerses it without a blessing, only the shopkeeper should inform the one who buys it from him afterward not to immerse it again with a blessing. What Rama wrote — that the first is forbidden to use for meal purposes, but for non-meal purposes it is permitted even though he took it for cards — does not require immersion; and conversely, if the second bought it for a meal, even though the first took it for cards and the like, nevertheless he requires immersion.
9#א: He immerses it. Meaning that he does not know whether the non-Jew intends to sink it in his possession or not; but if he knows clearly that the non-Jew does not intend to sink it, it is obvious that immersion is not required (Peri Chadash wrote that even if he knows clearly that the non-Jew does not intend to sink it, nevertheless he immerses without a blessing, and likewise Bach). However, where the non-Jew does not intend to sink it, Maharil wrote that one may not use it without the non-Jew's permission because of deception, which is forbidden even regarding a non-Jew's property; we do not practice thus but use a non-Jew's pledges even without permission even when known that he does not intend to sink them; likewise Taz, who saw in great communities on Sukkot that they use painted garments from non-Jewish pledges to decorate the sukkah and lend them to many others, and likewise covers — Heaven forbid to say they all transgress (likewise Peri Chadash; Beit Yosef wrote that specifically for cold items there is permission to use silver vessels, but not hot, because he causes loss — see there). In truth, even in Maharil he did not sign himself on this but perhaps the copyist heard and erred — end of Taz.
9#ב: It sank. Ohr U'Me'ir wrote; nevertheless, if he added money to the non-Jew and bought the pledge from him after they immersed it out of doubt, he requires immersion again with a blessing, for they did not immerse initially with this intent — accordingly (Peri Chadash disagrees and rules to immerse a second time also without a blessing).
10#א: Disagree. Shach wrote that Bach challenged Rama on this and his words are not plausible; the essential law is as Rama wrote, that even with Jewish silver, since the non-Jew makes the main vessel, immersion is required — whether the non-Jew makes an entirely new vessel or it was pierced and did not hold a revi'it, since the non-Jew stabilizes it, immersion is required even for Jewish silver, for a craftsman acquires through enhancement of the vessel; likewise Taz — see there (one should immerse without a blessing or with other vessels).
10#ב: Immersion. With a blessing — Shach; but Taz ruled to immerse without a blessing.
10#ג: Blessing. Because we are uncertain whether we follow the craftsman — and here immersion is not required — or we follow the one whose silver it is — Shach.
10#ד: His own. Shach wrote that it appears to him from Rama that when a Jew made it, even according to the view that we follow the one whose silver it is, it is possible where part of the silver is the Jew's that he agrees immersion is not required; but Taz wrote that it appears there is a scribal error here, and this "or he gave part of the money" belongs earlier; but if etc., and it teaches us two matters: first, that if the non-Jew gave all the metals, nevertheless he does not bless; and if he gave only part of his own, nevertheless immersion is required — end of his words (and see Peri Chadash).
11#א: He pledged it. Even if he intended to sink it in the non-Jew's possession, immersion is not required; Maharshal wrote that if initially he pledged it with intent not to redeem and then changed his mind and redeemed it, immersion is required; Taz wrote that although above there is doubt regarding a Jew who has a pledge from a non-Jew, here it is different, with proof from chapter Kol Sha'ah (Pesachim daf 41) that there is a dispute whether a Jew acquires a pledge from a non-Jew, and we say that a non-Jew from a Jew, however, does not acquire.
11#ב: In partnership. (For he certainly does not emerge from impurity through this immersion, for partnership of the non-Jew is still upon it.) And it implies that if the Jew returned and bought the non-Jew's share, immersion is required — Shach.
11#ג: They sank. Shach wrote that for a thief and robber, even though he despaired completely, since he is not permitted to hold it publicly, the non-Jew's name is not called upon it and immersion is not required; and likewise regarding a minister or governor, if he did not despair of them, likewise immersion is not required.
14#_: An adult. It implies from Rama's words that here we do not require intent at all (and likewise if a Jew immersed them afterward without the owner's knowledge, the immersion is valid) — Taz; and for this reason immersion by a non-Jew is effective b'dieved but not l'chatchila because of the blessing, unlike Bach who ruled that his immersion did not take effect, like a niddah — see siman 198; here it is different; accordingly, if vessels fell into water before their immersion they do not require immersion again — Shach; nevertheless Taz wrote that l'chatchila one should not immerse solely through a non-Jew, for how can he bless on what the non-Jew immerses; but if a Jew also immerses some vessel at that time while the non-Jew assists him to immerse the other vessels, the blessing refers to what the Jew does and it is fine — end of his words.
16#_: Mikveh. Taz wrote that after Shabbat or when a mikveh becomes available he must immerse it, even with a blessing; only since this is not explicit in the poskim one should be careful to immerse another vessel because of concern for a doubtful blessing; and see Orach Chaim siman 323 seif 7, where Rama wrote another remedy (to draw water in it from the mikveh and it counts as immersion, and the blessing does not prevent — see there). And see responsum of Maharal ibn Chaviv siman 16. Supplement to the laws of tevilat kelim — see below simanim 201 and 202.
